newsitem.title: UK: U.K. Labour victory could hurt ad agencies.
newsitem.headline: U.K. Labour victory could hurt ad agencies.

text.p: A victory by Britain's Labour Party in the next general election would likely spell bad news for advertising agencies but good news for public relations firms, according to a study released on Friday.

An expected total ban on tobacco advertising and greater restrictions on advertising to children would lower advertising rates, the advertising agency Ogilvy & Mather said in its "The Devil's in the Details" report.
But Labour's business policies would likely cause companies to be more concerned about their public image, boosting the fortunes of public relations firms, Ogilvy & Mather said.

The communications industry overall would be a winner under a Labour administration, the beneficiary of Labour's desire to use the information superhighway both to improve training and education throughout Britain and to make Britain a player in the international high-technology industry, the study concluded.

"You can no longer say that Labour is bad for business," David Muir, one of the report's co-authors, told a news conference. "If you are low-tech, low skill, low paying and unpopular don't expect any favours from them.
"But if you're hi-tech, high-skilled and popular with the public you're onto a winner," Muir said.

The Labour party, which has been leading Britain's ruling Conservative Party in public opinion polls for several months, is widely expected to win the next general election. Prime Minister John Major on Thursday said the next general election would at the latest be held on May 1, 1997. The last possible day the election can be held is May 22, 1997.

Labour, which has had an aversion to the advertising industry's tradition of self-regulation, is likely to impose greater controls -- both by using the threat of legislation to wring increased self-policing by the agency and by having greater pre-vetting of advertising.

"In view of Labour's past areas of concern, the categories most likely to come under closer scrutiny are financial services, tour operators, automotive and alcopops and, more generally, advertising to children," the report said.

Nigel Griffiths, the shadow consumer affairs minitster, recently told advertising officials that the Labour Party would not hesitate to use legislation to regulate products such as alcopops if self-regulation did not work.
The alcoholic beverage industry's advertisements for alcopops, highly sweetened alcoholic beverages, have drawn fire recently over concerns that they appeal to underage drinkers.

"Whatever the final proposals, tightening the rules will make it increasingly impractical to advertise to children," the Ogilvy & Mather report said. As a result, toy makers may turn to other means of promotion, such as sponsorship deals.

The Labour Party is also likely to come down hard on tobacco makers by implementing a total ban on tobacco advertising. Such a ban could, in turn, spark a ban on tobacco advertising by the European Union. Because the EU is now split about 50-50 on the tobacco advertising issue, a British ban could tip the scale in favour of a similar EU-wide ban, the report said.

"Removing tobacco advertising removes 20 percent of the revenue in the poster market, so prices will plummet," Muir told the news conference. "But it could be good news for advertisers in general because prices will be low," he added.
